Here's the exact trigger-action map you can build directly in Glide + Zapier (or Make) — no guesswork, just connect these:

## 🔗 Trigger-Action Map

### 1️⃣ New Job Created (Chatbot → App)
| Trigger | Action | Tool |
|---------|--------|------|
| Customer submits chatbot form | Create new row in "Repairs" sheet with Status = "New" | Zapier: Chatbase/Landbot → Google Sheets |
| New row appears in Repairs | Send WhatsApp/SMS confirmation: "We received your request, job #{ID}" | Zapier: Sheets → Twilio/WhatsApp API |

### 2️⃣ Job Status Changes
| Trigger | Action | Tool |
|---------|--------|------|
| Status changes to "In Progress" | Nothing external — just visible on dashboard | Glide native |
| Status changes to "Ready" | Send message: "Your phone is ready for pickup!" | Zapier: Sheets (row updated) → WhatsApp |
| Status changes to "Completed" | (a) Subtract 1 from Part quantity (b) Log revenue entry | Glide: Set Column Value action |

### 3️⃣ Inventory Automation
| Trigger | Action | Tool |
|---------|--------|------|
| Quantity ≤ Reorder Level (computed column) | Send alert to owner: "{Part} low — {Qty} left" | Zapier: Sheets filter → Email/WhatsApp |
| Owner marks "Restocked" checkbox | Reset quantity to new value, log restock date | Glide native |

### 4️⃣ Follow-Up & Reviews
| Trigger | Action | Tool |
|---------|--------|------|
| 7 days after "Completed" date | Send message: "How's your phone working?" | Zapier: Schedule/Delay → WhatsApp |
| 1 day after that (if no complaint) | Send: "Please leave us a review — here's 10% off" | Zapier: Delay → WhatsApp + Google Review link |

### 5️⃣ Predictive Restock (optional, later)
| Trigger | Action | Tool |
|---------|--------|------|
| Weekly scheduled run | Calculate average weekly usage per part → predict days until empty | Google Sheets formula or simple Python script |
| Prediction < 7 days | Trigger same low-stock alert flow | Same as #3 |

---

## 🛠️ Build order (do this sequence)

1. **Sheets first** — set up Repairs, Parts, Technicians tables with the columns already discussed.
2. **Glide app** — connect sheets, build views (Board by Status, Form for New Repair).
3. **Zapier account** — create these 5 zaps in order:
   - New row → WhatsApp confirmation
   - Status = Ready → WhatsApp message
   - Quantity ≤ Reorder → Alert
   - Completed + 7 days → Follow-up
   - Follow-up + 1 day → Review request
4. **Test with 3 dummy jobs** — walk them through New → In Progress → Ready → Completed, confirm every message fires correctly.
5. **Show shop owner** — this becomes your live demo.

Want me to write the actual Zapier setup screens (step-by-step what to click, what field to map) so you're not guessing inside Zapier's interface tomorrow?

The most important point in that whole map is **#2 — Job Status Changes**, specifically the moment when Status changes to "Completed."

Here's why this single trigger matters more than all the others combined, and why you should build it first and get it perfect before touching anything else.

## Why this is the core of the entire system

Every other automation is just *communication* — nice to have, makes the shop look professional. But the Completed-status trigger is where **money and inventory truth** actually happen. If this breaks or is inaccurate, the whole app becomes useless, because:

1. **It's the only place inventory updates automatically.** If a technician forgets to mark a job "Completed" — or marks it complete without logging which part was used — your stock count silently drifts from reality. After 2–3 weeks, the owner stops trusting the app ("it says I have 5 screens but I only have 2") and reverts to pen and paper. That's the #1 failure mode of every inventory app you'll ever build.

2. **It's the only place revenue gets logged.** If you're planning to eventually show the owner "you made €2,400 this month, here's the breakdown by technician/part/service," all of that traces back to this one trigger firing correctly and consistently.

3. **Every downstream automation depends on it.** The follow-up message (day 7), the review request (day 8), the predictive restock calculation — all of them use "Completed" as their starting timestamp. If this trigger is unreliable, everything built on top of it inherits that unreliability.

## How to make it bulletproof

- **Don't let "Completed" happen without "Part Used" filled in.** Make Part Used a required field before Status can be set to Completed (Glide supports conditional validation).
- **Log a timestamp automatically** the moment Status = Completed (not manually entered) — this becomes your single source of truth for the 7-day follow-up and any analytics.
- **Add a confirmation step for the technician**: after marking Completed, show a one-line summary ("iPhone 12 screen replacement — €80 — screen -1 unit") so they visually confirm before submitting. This catches human error before it corrupts your data.
- **Never allow manual quantity edits by staff** during daily use — only the automated subtraction and the weekly "Restocked" reset should touch quantity. Manual edits are how drift creeps in.

Get this one trigger rock-solid with your test jobs tomorrow before you even think about WhatsApp messages or review requests — those are polish, this is the foundation.

provider_responses.text:
Another aspect worth examining closely: **the low-stock alert accuracy problem** — specifically, the gap between what your Reorder Level *says* and what actually causes a shop to run out at the worst possible moment.

## Why this deserves more scrutiny than it got

The trigger-action map treats "Quantity ≤ Reorder Level" as a simple, solved problem. In practice, this is where the app will either earn trust or lose it fast, for reasons that aren't obvious until a shop actually uses it for a month.

### The static reorder level is a trap

If you set "iPhone 12 screen reorder level = 3" once and forget it, you're ignoring that demand isn't constant:

- A shop might sell 8 iPhone 12 screens one month (post-holiday cracked-screen wave) and 1 the next.
- A fixed threshold of "3" works fine in a slow month and fails completely in a busy one — the owner gets the alert, ignores it because "it's always low," then genuinely runs out mid-week and has to turn away a paying customer.
- This is worse than having no alert at all, because it trains the owner to distrust the notification ("the app cries wolf").

### What actually needs to happen

1. **Reorder level should scale with recent usage, not sit static.** Even a simple rule — "reorder level = 1.5x average weekly usage over last 4 weeks" — is far more useful than a number picked on day one.
2. **The alert needs urgency tiers, not just a binary flag.** "3 left, order this week" is different from "0 left, you will lose sales tomorrow." Right now the map treats these the same. Splitting into Warning / Critical changes owner behavior — critical alerts should probably escalate to SMS, not just an email that gets buried.
3. **Supplier lead time matters and isn't in the model at all.** If a part takes 5 days to arrive and the owner only gets alerted when 3 units are left but sells 2 a day, the alert is already too late by the time it fires. The reorder level calculation needs to factor in "how long until replacement arrives," not just current stock.

### The practical fix

Add one more column: **Lead Time (days)** per part (or per supplier). Then compute:

```
Reorder Level = (Average Daily Usage × Lead Time) + Safety Buffer
```

This single formula change is the difference between an app that *feels* smart and one that's just a spreadsheet with notifications bolted on. It's a small addition to your Parts table, but it's the actual intelligence layer that justifies calling this an "AI-assisted" inventory system rather than a glorified checklist.

This is worth getting right before you pitch a second or third shop — because the moment one owner runs out of a part *despite* your alert firing, you lose the credibility that makes this sellable at all.

Here's the concrete version — exact fields, exact formula, exact Zapier setup, ready to build in the next hour.

## 1️⃣ Add these 3 columns to your Parts sheet (in addition to what you already have)

| Column Name | Type | Example Value |
|---|---|---|
| Avg Daily Usage | Number (computed) | 0.6 |
| Lead Time Days | Number (manual entry, per part/supplier) | 4 |
| Safety Buffer | Number (manual, default 2) | 2 |

## 2️⃣ The actual formula (Google Sheets version, copy-paste ready)

In a new column called **"Smart Reorder Level"**:

```
=ROUNDUP((AvgDailyUsage * LeadTimeDays) + SafetyBuffer, 0)
```

To calculate **Avg Daily Usage** automatically (last 28 days), add this in the Repairs sheet or as a helper formula:

```
=COUNTIFS(Repairs!PartUsed, PartName, Repairs!CompletedDate, ">="&TODAY()-28) / 28
```

This counts how many times that part was used in the last 4 weeks and divides by 28 to get a daily rate.

## 3️⃣ Two-tier alert logic (instead of one flat alert)

Add a computed column **"Alert Level"**:

```
=IF(Quantity <= 0, "CRITICAL",
  IF(Quantity <= SmartReorderLevel, "WARNING", "OK"))
```

## 4️⃣ Exact Zapier setup (step by step, no guessing)

**Zap 1 — Warning alert (Email)**
- Trigger: Google Sheets → "New or Updated Spreadsheet Row" → watch Parts sheet
- Filter: Only continue if Alert Level = "WARNING"
- Action: Gmail/Email → Send to owner: *"Heads up: {Part Name} at {Quantity} units, expected to run out in ~{Quantity/AvgDailyUsage} days. Reorder soon."*

**Zap 2 — Critical alert (WhatsApp/SMS, more urgent channel)**
- Trigger: same sheet, same row watch
- Filter: Only continue if Alert Level = "CRITICAL"
- Action: Twilio/WhatsApp Business API → Send to owner's phone: *"URGENT: {Part Name} is OUT OF STOCK. Next repair needing this part will be delayed."*

This split matters practically: warnings can sit in email (owner checks once a day), but critical alerts need to interrupt them immediately, which is why it's a different channel entirely.

## 5️⃣ One real example to test with tomorrow

Say the shop uses iPhone 12 screens:
- Last 28 days: used in 17 repairs → Avg Daily Usage = 17/28 = 0.61
- Lead Time from supplier = 4 days
- Safety Buffer = 2

```
Smart Reorder Level = ROUNDUP((0.61 × 4) + 2, 0) = ROUNDUP(4.43, 0) = 5
```

So instead of an arbitrary "reorder at 3," the system tells the owner to reorder at **5** — because it now accounts for how fast they're actually selling through screens and how long the supplier takes to deliver.

## 6️⃣ What to do right now, in order

1. Open your Parts sheet, add the 3 new columns above.
2. Paste the two formulas (Smart Reorder Level, Alert Level).
3. Manually enter

provider_responses.text:
Here's what's likely being overlooked or misunderstood in everything discussed so far — the gaps that won't show up until real usage exposes them.

## 1️⃣ "Avg Daily Usage" breaks on low-volume parts

The formula `COUNTIFS(...) / 28` looks fine on paper, but most small repair shops don't sell 17 iPhone 12 screens a month — they sell 2 or 3. For a part used twice in 28 days:

```
Avg Daily Usage = 2/28 = 0.07
Smart Reorder Level = ROUNDUP((0.07 × 4) + 2, 0) = 3
```

That seems fine here, but for parts used *once* every two months, the math produces reorder levels near zero, meaning the alert never fires until the part is literally gone. **The formula quietly fails for slow-moving, expensive parts** — which are often exactly the ones that hurt most when unavailable (rare model screens, specific connectors). A minimum reorder level floor (e.g., "never let Smart Reorder Level go below 1") needs to be added, or these parts fall through completely.

## 2️⃣ New parts have no history — the formula divides by nothing meaningful

The moment the owner adds a brand-new part (new iPhone model just released), Avg Daily Usage = 0 for the first 28 days, so Smart Reorder Level = Safety Buffer only, regardless of real demand. This is invisible until a new iPhone drops, demand spikes immediately, and the "smart" system is dumber than a static number would've been. You need a manual override field ("Estimated Usage" for new parts) that the owner fills in once, which the formula falls back to when historical data is under, say, 14 days old.

## 3️⃣ The "Completed" trigger assumes one part per job — real repairs often use several

Every discussion so far treats "Part Used" as a single field. But a water-damage repair might use a battery *and* a charging port *and* cleaning supplies. If the schema only allows one Part Used per job, either:
- Technicians will only log the "main" part and the rest silently never gets subtracted from inventory (drift returns), or
- They'll create duplicate job entries to log multiple parts, which corrupts your revenue and analytics counts.

This needs a **multi-select or linked table** for parts-per-job, not a single text field — otherwise the core inventory-accuracy problem from earlier resurfaces through a different door.

## 4️⃣ Technician incentive is misaligned with data accuracy

Nothing in the system rewards a technician for logging carefully — it only adds friction (one more field, one more confirmation screen) to their workday. If they're paid per job completed, not per data quality, the fastest path is to rush through the form. The "confirmation summary before submitting" idea helps, but only if the owner also *spot-checks* physical stock against the app weekly for the first month. Without that human audit loop, small errors compound silently and nobody notices until a bigger discrepancy forces a manual recount — which is the exact failure mode the app was supposed to prevent.

## 5️⃣ WhatsApp/SMS costs and delivery aren't free or guaranteed

The critical-alert Zap assumes Twilio/WhatsApp messages just work. In practice: Twilio charges per message, WhatsApp Business API requires approval and a verified sender, and messages can fail silently if the owner's number isn't formatted correctly or opted in. If this is the *only* channel for critical stockout alerts, a failed message means the owner never finds out — the exact opposite of the point. A cheap safeguard: also show a red banner inside the Glide app it

Here's the clear path forward — just the essentials, in order:

## Fix these 4 things before building anything else

1. **Add a usage floor** — Smart Reorder Level should never go below 1, even if Avg Daily Usage is near zero. One line: `=MAX(SmartReorderLevel, 1)`

2. **Change Part Used to a linked/multi-select field**, not single text. One job can consume multiple parts. This is the single biggest data-integrity risk in the whole system — fix it now, before you have real jobs logged, because migrating data later is painful.

3. **Add a manual override field** for new parts with no usage history ("Estimated Weekly Usage") — formula falls back to this when historical data < 14 days old.

4. **Add a backup alert inside the app itself** (a red banner/badge on the Parts screen showing "CRITICAL" items), so if the WhatsApp/SMS message fails to send, the owner still sees it next time they open the app.

## Then do this, in order, starting tomorrow

1. Build the Parts, Repairs, Technicians sheets with the corrected schema (multi-part linking included).
2. Add the Smart Reorder Level formula with the floor and override built in.
3. Build the Glide app views — including the in-app critical alert banner.
4. Set up the two Zaps (Warning email, Critical WhatsApp).
5. Create 5 dummy jobs, deliberately including one with multiple parts and one brand-new part with no history — confirm both edge cases behave correctly.
6. Walk the owner through it in person, and agree on a **weekly manual stock spot-check** for the first month — this is non-negotiable, it's what catches the errors automation can't see.

That's the whole build, correctly ordered. Want the exact Glide field setup for the multi-part linked table next?

The most important point in that whole map is **#2 — Job Status Changes**, specifically the moment when Status changes to "Completed."

Here's why this single trigger matters more than all the others combined, and why you should build it first and get it perfect before touching anything else.

## Why this is the core of the entire system

Every other automation is just *communication* — nice to have, makes the shop look professional. But the Completed-status trigger is where **money and inventory truth** actually happen. If this breaks or is inaccurate, the whole app becomes useless, because:

1. **It's the only place inventory updates automatically.** If a technician forgets to mark a job "Completed" — or marks it complete without logging which part was used — your stock count silently drifts from reality. After 2–3 weeks, the owner stops trusting the app ("it says I have 5 screens but I only have 2") and reverts to pen and paper. That's the #1 failure mode of every inventory app you'll ever build.

2. **It's the only place revenue gets logged.** If you're planning to eventually show the owner "you made €2,400 this month, here's the breakdown by technician/part/service," all of that traces back to this one trigger firing correctly and consistently.

3. **Every downstream automation depends on it.** The follow-up message (day 7), the review request (day 8), the predictive restock calculation — all of them use "Completed" as their starting timestamp. If this trigger is unreliable, everything built on top of it inherits that unreliability.

## How to make it bulletproof

- **Don't let "Completed" happen without "Part Used" filled in.** Make Part Used a required field before Status can be set to Completed (Glide supports conditional validation).
- **Log a timestamp automatically** the moment Status = Completed (not manually entered) — this becomes your single source of truth for the 7-day follow-up and any analytics.
- **Add a confirmation step for the technician**: after marking Completed, show a one-line summary ("iPhone 12 screen replacement — €80 — screen -1 unit") so they visually confirm before submitting. This catches human error before it corrupts your data.
- **Never allow manual quantity edits by staff** during daily use — only the automated subtraction and the weekly "Restocked" reset should touch quantity. Manual edits are how drift creeps in.

Get this one trigger rock-solid with your test jobs tomorrow before you even think about WhatsApp messages or review requests — those are polish, this is the foundation.
Please examine another important aspect of the discussion.

Another aspect worth examining closely: **the low-stock alert accuracy problem** — specifically, the gap between what your Reorder Level *says* and what actually causes a shop to run out at the worst possible moment.

## Why this deserves more scrutiny than it got

The trigger-action map treats "Quantity ≤ Reorder Level" as a simple, solved problem. In practice, this is where the app will either earn trust or lose it fast, for reasons that aren't obvious until a shop actually uses it for a month.

### The static reorder level is a trap

If you set "iPhone 12 screen reorder level = 3" once and forget it, you're ignoring that demand isn't constant:

- A shop might sell 8 iPhone 12 screens one month (post-holiday cracked-screen wave) and 1 the next.
- A fixed threshold of "3" works fine in a slow month and fails completely in a busy one — the owner gets the alert, ignores it because "it's always low," then genuinely runs out mid-week and has to turn away a paying customer.
- This is worse than having no alert at all, because it trains the owner to distrust the notification ("the app cries wolf").

### What actually needs to happen

1. **Reorder level should scale with recent usage, not sit static.** Even a simple rule — "reorder level = 1.5x average weekly usage over last 4 weeks" — is far more useful than a number picked on day one.
2. **The alert needs urgency tiers, not just a binary flag.** "3 left, order this week" is different from "0 left, you will lose sales tomorrow." Right now the map treats these the same. Splitting into Warning / Critical changes owner behavior — critical alerts should probably escalate to SMS, not just an email that gets buried.
3. **Supplier lead time matters and isn't in the model at all.** If a part takes 5 days to arrive and the owner only gets alerted when 3 units are left but sells 2 a day, the alert is already too late by the time it fires. The reorder level calculation needs to factor in "how long until replacement arrives," not just current stock.

### The practical fix

Add one more column: **Lead Time (days)** per part (or per supplier). Then compute:

```
Reorder Level = (Average Daily Usage × Lead Time) + Safety Buffer
```

This single formula change is the difference between an app that *feels* smart and one that's just a spreadsheet with notifications bolted on. It's a small addition to your Parts table, but it's the actual intelligence layer that justifies calling this an "AI-assisted" inventory system rather than a glorified checklist.

This is worth getting right before you pitch a second or third shop — because the moment one owner runs out of a part *despite* your alert firing, you lose the credibility that makes this sellable at all.

Here's the concrete version — exact fields, exact formula, exact Zapier setup, ready to build in the next hour.

## 1️⃣ Add these 3 columns to your Parts sheet (in addition to what you already have)

| Column Name | Type | Example Value |
|---|---|---|
| Avg Daily Usage | Number (computed) | 0.6 |
| Lead Time Days | Number (manual entry, per part/supplier) | 4 |
| Safety Buffer | Number (manual, default 2) | 2 |

## 2️⃣ The actual formula (Google Sheets version, copy-paste ready)

In a new column called **"Smart Reorder Level"**:

```
=ROUNDUP((AvgDailyUsage * LeadTimeDays) + SafetyBuffer, 0)
```

To calculate **Avg Daily Usage** automatically (last 28 days), add this in the Repairs sheet or as a helper formula:

```
=COUNTIFS(Repairs!PartUsed, PartName, Repairs!CompletedDate, ">="&TODAY()-28) / 28
```

This counts how many times that part was used in the last 4 weeks and divides by 28 to get a daily rate.

## 3️⃣ Two-tier alert logic (instead of one flat alert)

Add a computed column **"Alert Level"**:

```
=IF(Quantity <= 0, "CRITICAL",
  IF(Quantity <= SmartReorderLevel, "WARNING", "OK"))
```

## 4️⃣ Exact Zapier setup (step by step, no guessing)

**Zap 1 — Warning alert (Email)**
- Trigger: Google Sheets → "New or Updated Spreadsheet Row" → watch Parts sheet
- Filter: Only continue if Alert Level = "WARNING"
- Action: Gmail/Email → Send to owner: *"Heads up: {Part Name} at {Quantity} units, expected to run out in ~{Quantity/AvgDailyUsage} days. Reorder soon."*

**Zap 2 — Critical alert (WhatsApp/SMS, more urgent channel)**
- Trigger: same sheet, same row watch
- Filter: Only continue if Alert Level = "CRITICAL"
- Action: Twilio/WhatsApp Business API → Send to owner's phone: *"URGENT: {Part Name} is OUT OF STOCK. Next repair needing this part will be delayed."*

This split matters practically: warnings can sit in email (owner checks once a day), but critical alerts need to interrupt them immediately, which is why it's a different channel entirely.

## 5️⃣ One real example to test with tomorrow

Say the shop uses iPhone 12 screens:
- Last 28 days: used in 17 repairs → Avg Daily Usage = 17/28 = 0.61
- Lead Time from supplier = 4 days
- Safety Buffer = 2

```
Smart Reorder Level = ROUNDUP((0.61 × 4) + 2, 0) = ROUNDUP(4.43, 0) = 5
```

So instead of an arbitrary "reorder at 3," the system tells the owner to reorder at **5** — because it now accounts for how fast they're actually selling through screens and how long the supplier takes to deliver.

Please consider what might be overlooked or misunderstood.

Here's what's likely being overlooked or misunderstood in everything discussed so far — the gaps that won't show up until real usage exposes them.

## 1️⃣ "Avg Daily Usage" breaks on low-volume parts

The formula `COUNTIFS(...) / 28` looks fine on paper, but most small repair shops don't sell 17 iPhone 12 screens a month — they sell 2 or 3. For a part used twice in 28 days:

```
Avg Daily Usage = 2/28 = 0.07
Smart Reorder Level = ROUNDUP((0.07 × 4) + 2, 0) = 3
```

That seems fine here, but for parts used *once* every two months, the math produces reorder levels near zero, meaning the alert never fires until the part is literally gone. **The formula quietly fails for slow-moving, expensive parts** — which are often exactly the ones that hurt most when unavailable (rare model screens, specific connectors). A minimum reorder level floor (e.g., "never let Smart Reorder Level go below 1") needs to be added, or these parts fall through completely.

## 2️⃣ New parts have no history — the formula divides by nothing meaningful

The moment the owner adds a brand-new part (new iPhone model just released), Avg Daily Usage = 0 for the first 28 days, so Smart Reorder Level = Safety Buffer only, regardless of real demand. This is invisible until a new iPhone drops, demand spikes immediately, and the "smart" system is dumber than a static number would've been. You need a manual override field ("Estimated Usage" for new parts) that the owner fills in once, which the formula falls back to when historical data is under, say, 14 days old.

## 3️⃣ The "Completed" trigger assumes one part per job — real repairs often use several

Every discussion so far treats "Part Used" as a single field. But a water-damage repair might use a battery *and* a charging port *and* cleaning supplies. If the schema only allows one Part Used per job, either:
- Technicians will only log the "main" part and the rest silently never gets subtracted from inventory (drift returns), or
- They'll create duplicate job entries to log multiple parts, which corrupts your revenue and analytics counts.

This needs a **multi-select or linked table** for parts-per-job, not a single text field — otherwise the core inventory-accuracy problem from earlier resurfaces through a different door.

## 4️⃣ Technician incentive is misaligned with data accuracy

Nothing in the system rewards a technician for logging carefully — it only adds friction (one more field, one more confirmation screen) to their workday. If they're paid per job completed, not per data quality, the fastest path is to rush through the form. The "confirmation summary before submitting" idea helps, but only if the owner also *spot-checks* physical stock against the app weekly for the first month. Without that human audit loop, small errors compound silently and nobody notices until a bigger discrepancy forces a manual recount — which is the exact failure mode the app was supposed to prevent.

## 5️⃣ WhatsApp/SMS costs and delivery aren't free or guaranteed

The critical-alert Zap assumes Twilio/WhatsApp messages just work. In practice: Twilio charges per message, WhatsApp Business API requires approval and a verified sender, and messages can fail silently if the owner's number isn't formatted correctly or opted in. If this is the *only* channel for critical stockout alerts, a failed message means the owner never finds out — the exact opposite of the point.
